one_line: Demonstrates how facial features are perceived holistically rather than in isolation, using chin and eyelid adjustments as examples.

hook.what_happens: A split-screen comparison of a woman's face with a slider, claiming only one feature was changed.
hook.why_it_works: Creates a visual puzzle that challenges the viewer's perception.

shots.description: A woman's face split vertically with a slider showing 'Before' and 'After' states.
Zoomed-in view highlighting the nose and chin areas with circular overlays.
A pixel-difference heatmap showing exactly which parts of the face changed.
Side-by-side comparison of nose and chin alignment using vertical measurement bars.
Second subject showing the effect of an upper blepharoplasty on eye perception.
Analysis of facial thirds and holistic facial reading using grid overlays.
Interactive prompt instructing the viewer to push their lower jaw forward.
Final call to action showing the Refina AI search bar mockup.

onscreen_text.text: This is the same face twice.
One thing on it was changed.
Almost everyone points at the nose.
Your eye reads a feature against everything around it.
This is every pixel that changed.
Almost none of them are on the nose.
It didn't shrink. The face caught up.
The nose and the chin are read as one
A chin that sits back leaves the nose out in front.
Bring the chin forward and the nose settles back.
Another face. The lid and the eye.
Skin resting on the lashes closes the eye beneath it.
Lift the hood and the eye reads open.
The eye didn't grow. The cover moved.
A face is read in thirds.
Move one boundary and all three change.
None of this tells you what to do.
It tells you why one feature can't answer it.
Faces are read whole. Not feature by feature.
So the question was never one feature.
It's what the whole face does when it moves.
See it on your own face first.

transcript.text: This is the same face twice. One thing on it was changed.
Almost everyone points at the nose. The nose isn't what changed. The chin is.
Your eye reads a feature against everything around it.
This is every pixel that changed. Almost none of them are on the nose.
It didn't shrink. The face caught up.
One. The nose and the chin are read as one line.
A chin that sits back leaves the nose out in front. Bring the chin forward and the nose settles back. Same nose. Every time.
Two. Another face. The lid and the eye.
Skin resting on the lashes closes the eye beneath it. Lift the hood and the eye reads open. The eye didn't grow. The cover moved.
Three. A face is read in thirds. Hairline to brow. Brow to nose. Nose to chin.
Move one boundary and all three change.
None of this tells you what to do. It tells you why one feature can't answer it. Faces are read whole. Not feature by feature.
Push your lower jaw forward a few millimetres. Hold it. Now look at your nose. Watch your nose get smaller. You didn't touch your nose.
So the question was never one feature. It's what the whole face does when it moves.

narrative_arc: Introduce a visual puzzle challenging the viewer's perception of facial changes.
Reveal that changing the chin alters the perception of the nose.
Provide scientific/visual proof using pixel-change heatmaps.
Explain the relationship between facial features (nose/chin, lid/eye, facial thirds).
Engage the viewer with an interactive physical test they can do immediately.
Introduce the product (Refina AI) as a tool to preview these holistic changes.

cta.what: Search 'Refina AI' to see holistic facial previews on your own face.

subjects: Unnamed female subject (primary model for chin/nose and facial thirds analysis)
Unnamed older Black female subject (model for eyelid/eye analysis)
what_makes_it_work: The interactive 'try it now' jaw-thrust exercise immediately proves the video's thesis to the viewer.
High-quality, clinical-style visual overlays build scientific authority.
The counter-intuitive hook keeps viewers watching to find out the trick.

what_we_should_steal: Facial Thirds Grid (TrimPath) - Excellent for technical, structured breakdowns.
Pixel Change Heatmap (Reveal) - Highly effective way to show subtle differences.
